title: Al-Qayyum, the Self-Subsisting
tomorrow: "did He not find thee...?" find you how, exactly?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Hayy: tears and steadiness, side by side in one sentence. The line: ever-living. And a question: the verse says He never sleeps. Why would that help us sleep?

Somewhere tonight a nurse, a power-plant tech and an air traffic controller are on the night shift. They stay awake so a whole city can sleep, and nobody downtown knows their names. Ayat al-Kursi has that shape. Right after the Alive comes today's Name, Al-Qayyum, and then the line from yesterday: neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him. Someone is always on shift. That's the answer. Because He doesn't sleep, we can.
screen: `THE NIGHT SHIFT.` → `AWAKE SO OTHERS CAN SLEEP.` → `BECAUSE HE DOESN'T, WE CAN.`

segments.voice: Pickthall renders Al-Qayyum as the Eternal, but the word reaches further: the one who stands by Himself, needing nothing, and holds everything else up. Surah Fatir puts it in a picture: "Lo! Allah graspeth the heavens and the earth that they deviate not." Nothing in creation stands on its own. Not the sky, not the ground, not the person who has been holding a family together all week. There's a reason Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi at bedtime: a hadith says that whoever recites it on going to bed has a guardian from Allah through the night. And there's a du'a the Prophet, peace be upon him, taught, built on these two Names: Ya Hayyu ya Qayyum, O Ever-Living, O Self-Subsisting, by Your mercy I seek help. In one version it goes on: set right all my affairs, and don't leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye. Here's the line to tell a friend tonight. That prayer doesn't ask to be made stronger. It asks not to be left alone with only yourself to lean on. Leaning isn't the failure. Leaning is what creatures are built to do.
screen: `STANDS BY HIMSELF, HOLDS ALL ELSE UP.` · `HE GRASPETH THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH.` · `A GUARDIAN THROUGH THE NIGHT.` · `NOT LEFT TO MYSELF, NOT FOR A BLINK.` · then, large: `HE HOLDS IT UP.`

segments.voice: Sit back so a wall or the back of your chair takes your full weight. Let your shoulders drop, then your arms, then your jaw, until you're not holding yourself up at all. For the two minutes, notice how much was being carried for you the whole time.
screen: `LET THE WALL TAKE YOUR WEIGHT.` · `SHOULDERS, ARMS, JAW.`

segments.voice: Al-Qayyum. The Self-Subsisting: needing nothing, holding up everything, awake while the city sleeps.
Something to lean on: he holds it up, the sky, the night, and whoever is holding everything else. Sleep well tonight.
